https://www.politico.eu/article/greece-e.text: Greek farmers claimed EU subsidies for tens of thousands more farm animals in 2024 than the country’s official records can account for, according to a POLITICO analysis of government data. The finding threatens to expand a wider Greek farm-subsidy scandal . The analysis reveals discrepancies between a shrinking national cattle herd as reported by ELSTAT, Greece’s statistics agency, and the subsidies recorded by the Greek agriculture ministry. Recent farm scandals have prompted the Athens government to promise overhauls and increase controls over agriculture. “Greek livestock farming is turning a new page,” Agriculture Minister Margaritis Schinas said at a press conference in June. “It is fulfilling its commitments to the EU and entering a new era in the agriculture sector — one governed by rules, transparency and reliability.” But the data discrepancies suggest there is further to go before the government has enough information to get a grip on the issue. For 2024, data from the agriculture ministry shows that the Greek authorities paid out EU subsidies for about 260,000 lactating cows, according to figures cited by a Greek agricultural news site and confirmed by POLITICO with the agricultural ministry. Advertisement Because a lactating cow generally produces one calf a year, those cows should have added roughly the same number of calves to the national herd. The agriculture ministry data also shows that during 2024 about 70,000 cattle were slaughtered for meat, which also qualifies for subsidies. Greece does not publish comprehensive figures for cattle that are culled because of age, declining productivity or disease. But three Greek cattle breeders told POLITICO that such removals amount to roughly 20 percent of the herd each year. Given that there were about 600,000 head of cattle in Greece in 2024, according to ELSTAT , that would be a decrease of about 120,000 animals. Taken with the subsidies data, that estimate suggests the national herd should have grown by roughly 70,000 that year. The Mornos artificial lake, near the village of Lidoriki, about 240 km northwest of Athens. | Angelos Tzortzinis/AFP via Getty Images Instead, data compiled by ELSTAT through annual surveys show the national herd has been shrinking , from about 640,000 in 2023 to 600,000 in 2024 to 520,000 in 2025, according to the most recent figures published in June. The discrepancy could be even larger, said Nikos Dimopoulos, chair of the Kavala Livestock Farmers’ Association. For instance, some of the animals that were slaughtered might have been imported rather than removed from the national herd. In most years, Greece is a net importer of live cattle and exports only small numbers. “There’s no oversight and we cannot have an exact figure because there is no accurate data,” Dimopoulos said. Authorities only carry out spot checks or investigate following a complaint. Advertisement Similar discrepancies appear in Greece’s sheep and goat records. ELSTAT reported a population of about 8.8 million animals in 2025, while some 15.7 million were registered in the country’s Integrated Veterinary Information System, a government database . Two agriculture ministry officials, granted anonymity because they were not authorized to comment on the issue, said the ministry is not responsible for maintaining livestock records and relies on data supplied by municipalities. The country lacks a secure and reliable registry on which to base the payment of livestock subsidies, experts say. “Unless we carry out a nationwide census of livestock to see what we actually have, we will not have a clear picture,” Dimopoulos said. Cows that appear to have fire burn wounds try to relocate during a wildfire in Velestino July 26, 2023. | Nephele Nomikou via Getty Images Complaints about the discrepancy between the recorded subsidies and the official size of the national cattle herd have been submitted to the European Public Prosecutor’s Office by the recently formed left-wing Elas party of former Prime Minister Alexis Tsipras, which conducted its own study of livestock numbers. “Complaints have been sent to EPPO,” said Thomas Moschos, who heads the party’s agriculture policy. He added that the Agricultural Association of Kastoria, a small-scale farmers’ organization where he serves as president, along with other associations have already submitted cases to the authority. EPPO, which declined to confirm it was examining the matter, is already pursuing dozens of cases involving people who allegedly received EU agricultural funds for pastureland they did not own or lease, or for farming work they did not perform. Advertisement In July the agency announced it had indicted 22 defendants, including four lawmakers from the ruling New Democracy party, as part of its investigation into agricultural fraud. The trials for the lawmakers begin in Athens in October. They all deny any wrongdoing. Veterinarians and officials at OPEKEPE — the agency formerly responsible for distributing EU agricultural funds that was shut down due to the farm-subsidy scandal — allegedly played a role in inflating livestock records, according to a document EPPO submitted to the Greek parliament asking it to lift the immunity of several lawmakers. One EPPO case involving a New Democracy lawmaker concerns alleged subsidy payments to a breeder for more cows than he actually owned. According to the case file seen by POLITICO, the lawmaker called a senior OPEKEPE official to press for the payment and said a veterinarian had already altered the breeder’s animal numbers in the official veterinary database, increasing the subsidy for which he was eligible. The case will be heard on Oct. 2. A cow farm in the village of Melanes on the island of Naxos. | Martin Bertrand and Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images The scandal has prompted the government to introduce new controls such as an electronic identification system for sheep and goats using stomach capsules, known as boluses. The system is due to be piloted this year on farms with more than 900 animals, covering about 700,000 sheep and goats, before being expanded in subsequent years. In March, Greece submitted an action plan to EU authorities setting out measures to prevent agricultural funds from being wrongfully doled out. The European Commission said it would work with Greece to help “further improve the management” of European farming subsidies. “Good progress is taking place,” Agriculture Commissioner Christophe Hansen said in a written statement. “But there is still work to be done.” Advertisement

https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text: Brandram was arrested in June on suspicion of attempted grievous bodily harm, nine years after a jogger shoved a woman into the path of a bus in London. Photograph: Family handout/PA View image in fullscreen Brandram was arrested in June on suspicion of attempted grievous bodily harm, nine years after a jogger shoved a woman into the path of a bus in London. Photograph: Family handout/PA London Suspect in ‘Putney pusher’ case told family that investigation was ‘murdering him’ Exclusive: Sisters of Nicholas Brandram recount 44-year-old’s deteriorating mental health in days before he took his life Emine Sinmaz Thu 17 Sep 2026 16.33 EDT Last modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 16.38 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Days before Nicholas Brandram, the man suspected of being the “Putney pusher”, killed himself, he told his family that the police investigation was “murdering him”. He had “no fight left” in him, he told his sisters, Alexia Hicks and Sophie Voelcker, and could not see an end to the Metropolitan police investigation, or the online abuse. Brandram’s lawyers warned the Met last week that his mental health had deteriorated and he was receiving treatment in a psychiatric hospital after renewed press reporting that he had been released under investigation. “He said a couple of days ago that this investigation was murdering him. Day by day, he was slowly being murdered,” Hicks, 40, said through tears. “He saw no end to this investigation,” added Voelcker, 45. “My sister and I were keeping a close eye on him because he was telling us he couldn’t go on. He said it more than once in the week before, that he couldn’t keep going. All we could do was just reassure him. We had faith in the system, we had faith in the police, and they neglected him. They failed in their duty of care to him, to the wider family, and we do not want to see another family going through this.” The pair insisted that Brandram, 44, was not the “Putney pusher” and that he died thinking no one would believe in his innocence. He was arrested on suspicion of attempted grievous bodily harm on 15 June, nine years after a jogger shoved a woman headfirst into the path of an oncoming bus on Putney Bridge in south-west London. The case attracted considerable media attention but appeared to elude detectives, who wound down their investigation in 2018, after interviewing 50 men and arresting three suspects. But there was renewed interest in the case after Brandram’s arrest, which his family described as heavy-handed and disproportionate. A number of officers in body armour reportedly swooped on his home address, his sisters said, while a reporter who had been tipped off about the arrest filmed the ordeal. Although Brandram’s name was not published in the media because he had not been charged, his family said that biographical information in reports made him easily identifiable. He was described as a wealthy banker who lived in a £1.4m west London home and an army veteran with links to royalty. Brandram was the grandson of Princess Katherine of Greece, who was a great-granddaughter of Queen Victoria, which made his arrest all the more newsworthy. View image in fullscreen From left to right: Nicholas Brandram, Alexia Hicks and Sophie Voelcker as children. Photograph: Family handout While in police custody in June over the Putney Bridge incident, he was also arrested on suspicion of possession of class A and class B drugs. His sisters said there was no forensic evidence linking Brandram to the Putney incident and that he had a prominent military tattoo and a withered calf which, they said, distinguished him from the man in footage of the attack on 5 May 2017. That morning, Brandram had walked from his home in Notting Hill Gate to his office in Bond Street and sent his sisters an email from his work account, which they said he could only access from his workplace. They said that evidence was passed on to the police. They added that Brandram had volunteered to take part in an identification parade and provided his DNA for comparison with a sample recovered at the time of the incident. Hicks said detectives told Brandram just days ago that they still did not know when the DNA analysis would be completed. “Our brother willingly provided DNA in an attempt to obviously help clear his name and to complete the investigation, and for weeks now we’ve been asking the police just to complete the DNA test,” Voelcker said. “We’ve always maintained that he’s innocent. He always maintained he was innocent. We just needed the police to complete their inquiry, and it just felt particularly egregious that they were just hanging this DNA test over him.” Hicks said as details of the case kept being reported in the press, her brother became preoccupied by online abuse on forums such as Reddit. “His reputation within a couple of days was in tatters. People saying he’s the alleged pusher, and you can imagine the vitriol that was coming out online,” Voelcker said. “You can imagine what people might say about somebody they think tried to push a woman in front of a bus. There was a lot of people had a lot of views about our brother, about his background, about where he worked.” “And the problem was he was reading it all every day,” Hicks said. “The vitriol is still there and that’s what’s so heartbreaking for us, is that when he took his own life he died thinking that effectively everyone hated him and thought he’d done something awful and that no one would see that he was innocent and he knew that his family were behind him but it wasn’t enough.” The sisters said Brandram had stayed with them in recent days after his mental health deteriorated following the publication of an update about the case that said he had been released under investigation. “He was really talking about ending his life and ending things. And he was very low and said he felt like he had no fight left in him. He couldn’t see the end,” Voelcker said. Brandram was admitted to a psychiatric hospital for six days before being discharged on Sunday. His family insisted the Met police were warned about his mental health. Voelcker tried to boost his mood on Tuesday by telling him it was a beautiful day and that he had many friends and his family supporting him. He was found dead at his home in Chiswick, west London, later that day. The family said their priority was to clear their brother’s name and “to ensure another family does not have to go through what we have as a result of the police delays and leaks to the media”. Hicks said: “Nick was really very loving, enthusiastic. He had an infectious character to be around, very funny. He was an extrovert, so he loved people. He was a much-loved father and uncle.” Voelcker added: “He spent a long time in the army before going into the city. And his reputation was important. He was a proud man. I think that’s the thing and even the fact that he needed to seek help from a psychiatric hospital was a big deal for him.” Ch Supt Dan Knowles, in charge of policing for south-west London, said: “Our thoughts are with Mr Brandram’s family and friends at this deeply distressing time. We recognise the significant impact his death will have on those who knew and loved him. We also understand the strain that being subject to a police investigation can place on individuals and their families. “The investigation remains ongoing. Following Mr Brandram’s release under investigation, it was made clear that inquiries would continue while officers progressed outstanding lines of inquiry and forensic examinations. This remains the position, and further investigative work is ongoing. “Investigations of this nature, particularly those involving complex evidential and forensic work, can take a number of months to complete as officers gather and assess all available evidence.” He added that the force had made a mandatory referral to the Independent Office for Police Conduct on 16 September. https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text: Wasim El-Haj, a former careers adviser at Sydney Girls High School, is suing NSW for racial discrimination after allegedly being ordered to stop wearing a keffiyeh at the school. Photograph: The Guardian View image in fullscreen Wasim El-Haj, a former careers adviser at Sydney Girls High School, is suing NSW for racial discrimination after allegedly being ordered to stop wearing a keffiyeh at the school. Photograph: The Guardian New South Wales Palestinian careers adviser who was allegedly told to stop wearing keffiyeh at Sydney school sues for racial discrimination Wasim El-Haj alleges NSW government school ordered him to stop wearing symbolic garment as it ‘may cause discord’ Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Adeshola Ore Community affairs reporter Sat 26 Sep 2026 16.00 EDT Last modified on Sat 26 Sep 2026 16.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A Palestinian careers adviser who was allegedly directed to stop wearing a keffiyeh at a Sydney government school because it was a symbol that “may cause discord” has lodged a racial discrimination case in the federal court against the state of New South Wales . Wasim El-Haj, a former careers adviser at Sydney Girls High School – an inner-city selective government school – alleges the then acting principal told him in 2024 that the keffiyeh was seen as a symbol of conflict. He alleges the state’s conduct is unlawful for breaching the Racial Discrimination Act. El-Haj began wearing the keffiyeh – a traditional scarf linked to the struggle for a Palestinian state for decades – at school in January 2024, three months after Hamas’ 7 October attacks and Israel’s subsequent war on Gaza. His statement of claim, filed in the federal court last month, alleges Geoffrey Denyer, the then acting school principal, met with him on 15 May 2024 and said words to the effect of “I have been directed to direct you to remove this item of clothing”, indicating to El-Haj’s keiffeyh. View image in fullscreen Wasim El-Haj began wearing the keffiyeh to Sydney Girls High School in January 2024. Photograph: The Guardian Denyer also said words to the effect of the direction had come “from above, possibly from the minister” and that action would be taken if El-Haj did not comply, the statement of claim alleges. In an email sent the same day, after El-Haj requested the issue be laid out in writing, Denyer outlined the terms of the direction he had received. “Consistent with the Department’s Controversial Issues and Code of Conduct policies, the staff member in question should be given clear advice, from you, that this item of clothing should not be worn at school, nor in the performance of any duties in connection with his employment. That advice should be complied with immediately,” the email said. “It is understandable that, in such times as these, feelings and emotions are strong. However, our schools need to remain free of symbols which stir these emotions, and which may cause discord.” Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email El-Haj alleges that in a further conversation with Denyer he said words to the effect of “any symbol of Palestine is seen as a symbol of conflict”. In August 2024, El-Haj met with Maria Serafim, a NSW Department of Education official, who detailed six anonymous concerns, including that he had worn a symbol of “partisan conflict” by wearing the keffiyeh, the statement of claim alleges. An internal complaint El-Haj made about the direction did not lead to its withdrawal. The careers advisor appealed the decision about the complaint to the secretary of the NSW Department of Education, Murat Dizdar. Responding to this, Dizdar upheld the school’s decision. In a letter to El-Haj in February 2025, he recognised the keffiyeh “is a garment of cultural significance for the Palestinian community” but said the department did not want to compromise the “safety, wellbeing and security in all our school communities”. View image in fullscreen Wasim El-Haj says he was told words to the effect of ‘any symbol of Palestine is seen as a symbol of conflict’. Photograph: The Guardian “Unfortunately, our schools are not immune to external events, such as the ongoing conflict in the Middle East, with the tragic loss of innocent lives,” he said. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion “Regrettably, within our school communities, some individuals and groups may seek to politicise global conflicts or others may form that perception, and as such we always remain politically neutral in public schools when such events can impact on operations. “It is with this context that the senior officers and the school advised you to not wear the keffiyeh to school.” El-Haj took leave from his employment from May 2024 until the end of the year and resigned from Sydney Girls High School in March 2025. El-Haj alleges the state of NSW has engaged in unlawful conduct under section 9(1) of the Racial Discrimination Act. The state of NSW is yet to file its defence in the federal court. The matter is due to be next heard for a case management hearing on 3 November, federal court records show. A spokesperson for the NSW Department of Education said it was “committed to maintaining neutral and apolitical school environments, in line with its policies.” Guardian Australia understands the department is not able to make further comments while the matter is before court.
